submission.natural_language_explanation: The pole fires on concrete, particular description: activation is elevated across the tokens of a passage that depicts a specific situation - particular people, animals, objects or places and what they are doing - and it peaks on specific times of day inside such text ('at 10:30', 'ten thirty', "nine o'clock"), which reach roughly half to all of max even in otherwise abstract prose. Abstract, generic, definitional, instructional, summarizing or technical prose stays at or near zero, and bare dates, prices, counts or proper names without a situation do not raise it above the activity threshold.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Researchers who study institutional decision-making have long noted that the written record of a meeting rarely matches the substance of what was said. Minutes condense, paraphrase and omit, and the resulting document is shaped by genre conventions as much as by events. A recurring observation in the literature is that the more consequential a decision, the more generic its written justification tends to become. Committees adopt the passive voice. They attribute judgment to unnamed bodies. They record that options were considered, that stakeholders were consulted, and that further work is required. None of this is dishonest; it is simply the register in which organizations speak about themselves. The same pattern appears across sectors, from municipal planning to hospital governance, and it complicates any attempt to reconstruct a decision from the archive alone. Historians of administration have therefore developed methods of reading against the grain of such documents, comparing successive drafts, cross-referencing correspondence, and attending closely to what a text declines to specify. The method has limits. Surviving records are unrepresentative, and silence can be caused by loss as easily as by intention. Nonetheless the general finding is robust: abstraction in institutional prose is functional rather than accidental, and it increases in proportion to the sensitivity of the matter at hand. A second body of work examines how such documents are summarized in turn. Summaries of summaries lose further specificity, and after two or three iterations an account may contain no particulars at all, only categories and conclusions. This is not merely an aesthetic complaint. It has practical consequences for accountability, since the absence of particulars makes it harder to establish who decided what, and on what grounds. Scholars in this tradition sometimes contrast the archival record with other traces of the same events: correspondence, diaries, marginalia, and the physical layout of the rooms in which decisions were made. Each carries its own conventions, and none is straightforwardly transparent, but together they can restore a measure of specificity to an otherwise abstract record. The methodological point is that no single genre can be read as a simple window onto events; the analyst must weigh several registers against one another and be explicit about the inferential steps that connect a document to a claim. On the morning the committee finally voted, the rain had stopped and the caretaker was still mopping the entrance hall. Mrs. Adeyemi arrived early with a cardboard folder under her arm and sat in the third row, tapping her pen against her teeth. When the chair called the item, she stood, walked to the lectern, and read the paragraph she had written the night before. Behind her a fluorescent tube flickered each time the heating came on. The vote was taken in under a minute, the folder was closed, and she walked back out into the car park without speaking to anyone. A scene of that kind would never enter the official record in that form. What survives is a single line noting that the item was approved, and perhaps a name in an attendance list. The gap between the event and its trace is the ordinary condition of the archive, and it is the reason computational summaries of institutional text must be read with the same caution as the documents they compress.
